triage.reason: Early pregnancy bleeding/cramping case with clear workup (hCG, ultrasound) and important differential of ectopic pregnancy.

demographics: Occurs in about 10–20% of recognized pregnancies
Risk rises steadily with maternal age, especially after 35

risk_factors.text: Uterine or cervical structural problems (fibroids, septum, cervical insufficiency)
Smoking, alcohol or illicit drug use
Severe malnutrition or very low body weight

family_history: Recurrent pregnancy loss in a first-degree relative
exposures: Invasive prenatal procedures (amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling)

chief_complaints.text: I'm bleeding down there and I'm pregnant
I've been having bad cramps in my belly
I passed some tissue in the toilet

hpi.onset: Gradual, over hours to days; bleeding is usually the first sign
hpi.duration: Symptoms typically present within days of onset; most miscarriages occur before 12 weeks
hpi.progression: Spotting or light bleeding progresses to heavier bleeding with clots and cramping; tissue may pass; symptoms may resolve or continue depending on whether the pregnancy has fully passed
hpi.location: Lower abdomen and pelvis, often with low back pain
hpi.radiation: Cramping may radiate to the lower back or sacrum
hpi.quality: Crampy, period-like pelvic pain with vaginal bleeding
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; can become severe if heavy bleeding or incomplete passage occurs
hpi.timing: Intermittent cramping that comes in waves; bleeding may be continuous

associated_symptoms.text: Passage of grayish or pinkish tissue
Gush of clear or pink fluid from the vagina
Loss of pregnancy symptoms such as breast tenderness or nausea
Dizziness or lightheadedness with heavy bleeding

positives.text: Anxiety or sadness about the pregnancy

atypical.how_it_differs: Women over 40 have a higher baseline risk and may present with earlier or more subtle bleeding; they are also more likely to have comorbid conditions such as fibroids or chronic disease.
missing_classic_features: Clear temporal relationship to a missed period

atypical.how_it_differs: Poorly controlled diabetes increases risk and can make bleeding and cramping harder to distinguish from other pregnancy complications.
Obesity is associated with higher miscarriage risk and may make pelvic examination and ultrasound visualization more difficult.

general.mild: Alert, comfortable, no distress; normal affect
general.moderate: Mild discomfort, cramping with movement, anxious
general.severe: Pale, diaphoretic, visibly uncomfortable, guarding the lower abdomen
general.critical: Ill-appearing, pale, clammy, lethargic, signs of hypovolemic shock

labs.caveat: Quantitative serum hCG confirms pregnancy and, when followed serially, shows a suboptimal rise or fall. A single value cannot distinguish miscarriage from a normal early pregnancy or an ectopic; a plateau or slow rise raises concern for ectopic pregnancy.
Falls with significant blood loss; a normal value early does not exclude ongoing hemorrhage.
Thrombocytopenia raises concern for a coagulopathy such as disseminated intravascular coagulation in septic abortion or placental abruption.
Mild leukocytosis can be normal in pregnancy; marked elevation with fever suggests septic abortion.
Rises with hypovolemia from heavy bleeding; baseline is lower in pregnancy.
Prolongation supports a coagulopathy in heavy bleeding or suspected septic abortion.
Low fibrinogen supports disseminated intravascular coagulation in heavy bleeding.
Elevation with fever and uterine tenderness suggests septic abortion.
Blood from vaginal bleeding can contaminate the specimen; not specific for urinary pathology.

findings.finding: Sinus tachycardia from pain, anxiety or hypovolemia

imaging.preferred_when: First-line in early pregnancy (before about 12 weeks)

Assesses hydration and renal function when bleeding is heavy
Screens for urinary infection or other causes of pelvic pain and bleeding

decision_points: Confirm pregnancy with a quantitative hCG before imaging
Transvaginal ultrasound is the first-line test to distinguish miscarriage from ectopic pregnancy
If the uterus is empty and hCG is above the discriminatory zone, ectopic pregnancy must be excluded
Serial hCG levels are used when the initial ultrasound is nondiagnostic
Rh-negative women with bleeding receive anti-D immune globulin
Fever, uterine tenderness or foul discharge suggests septic abortion and requires antibiotics and uterine evacuation

differential.name: Ectopic pregnancy
differential.why_considered: Early pregnancy with vaginal bleeding and cramping pelvic pain; the single most important diagnosis to exclude because it can rupture and cause fatal hemorrhage.
differential.trigger: Any pregnant patient with bleeding or pelvic pain, especially unilateral pain, an empty uterus on ultrasound, or an hCG above the discriminatory zone

history: Unilateral, sharp or stabbing pelvic pain rather than central cramping
Shoulder tip pain or pain worse with movement
History of pelvic inflammatory disease, prior ectopic, tubal surgery, or intrauterine device use
Syncope or near-syncope
exam: Focal adnexal tenderness or a palpable adnexal mass
Signs of hypovolemia out of proportion to visible bleeding
labs: hCG that plateaus or rises suboptimally on serial testing
imaging: Empty uterus with no intrauterine gestational sac despite hCG above the discriminatory zone
Extrauterine gestational sac, adnexal mass, or free fluid in the pelvis

differential.name: Threatened miscarriage
differential.why_considered: Vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy with a closed cervix and a viable intrauterine pregnancy; it is the same clinical spectrum and must be distinguished from an inevitable or completed loss.

history: Light spotting or bleeding without passage of tissue
Cramping absent or mild
Symptoms may resolve with rest
labs: hCG rising appropriately on serial testing
imaging: Intrauterine gestational sac with a live embryo and cardiac activity

differential.name: Septic abortion
differential.why_considered: Retained products of conception with uterine infection can present with bleeding and cramping and can progress to sepsis and death if not recognized.
differential.trigger: Fever, foul-smelling vaginal discharge, uterine tenderness, or hemodynamic instability after passage of tissue or instrumentation

history: Fever and chills
Foul-smelling vaginal discharge
Recent uterine instrumentation or incomplete passage of tissue
Worsening pelvic pain
exam: Purulent or foul discharge from the cervical os
labs: Thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy in severe cases
imaging: Retained products of conception within the uterus
Gas within the uterus on ultrasound in severe cases

differential.name: Molar pregnancy
differential.why_considered: Abnormal pregnancy with bleeding, passage of grapelike tissue, and a uterus larger than expected; can mimic miscarriage but carries risk of persistent trophoblastic disease.
differential.trigger: Uterus larger than dates, very high hCG, passage of grapelike vesicles, or severe vomiting in early pregnancy

history: Passage of grapelike or vesicular tissue
Severe nausea and vomiting
Symptoms of hyperthyroidism or early preeclampsia
exam: Uterus larger than expected for gestational age
Possible theca lutein cysts on pelvic exam
labs: Markedly elevated hCG, often far above expected for gestational age
Elevated free T4 or suppressed TSH
imaging: Snowstorm or cluster of grapes appearance on ultrasound
Theca lutein cysts of the ovaries

differential.name: Implantation bleeding
differential.why_considered: Light spotting in early pregnancy that can be mistaken for the start of a miscarriage.

history: Very light spotting, often brown, lasting hours to a couple of days
Occurs around the time of expected menses
No cramping or only mild twinges
imaging: Viable intrauterine pregnancy with cardiac activity

differential.name: Subchorionic hematoma
differential.why_considered: Blood collection between the chorion and uterine wall causing bleeding and cramping in early pregnancy; may coexist with or precede miscarriage.

history: Sudden onset of bleeding, sometimes heavier than spotting
Cramping may be present but mild
labs: hCG rising appropriately if pregnancy is viable
imaging: Echogenic or anechoic collection between the gestational sac and uterine wall

differential.name: Cervical insufficiency
differential.why_considered: Painless cervical dilation in the second trimester leading to passage of tissue and pregnancy loss; can present similarly to miscarriage but with a different mechanism and management.

history: Painless cervical dilation or bulging membranes
History of second-trimester loss or prior cervical surgery
Often no or minimal cramping before rupture of membranes
exam: Open cervix with visible membranes or tissue
labs: Signs of infection if membranes have been ruptured
imaging: Shortened cervical length on transvaginal ultrasound
Bulging membranes into the cervical canal

differential.name: Urinary tract infection
differential.why_considered: Can cause pelvic discomfort and sometimes hematuria that is mistaken for vaginal bleeding in pregnancy.

history: Dysuria, urgency, frequency
Suprapubic discomfort rather than cramping
No passage of tissue
exam: No vaginal bleeding on speculum exam
labs: Positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites on urinalysis
imaging: Not routinely needed; ultrasound may show viable pregnancy if obtained

severity.mild: Threatened miscarriage: light spotting, closed cervix, mild or no cramping, hemodynamically stable, viable pregnancy possible on ultrasound
severity.moderate: Incomplete or inevitable miscarriage: heavier bleeding with clots, open cervix or tissue at the os, moderate cramping, stable vitals, no signs of infection
severity.severe: Heavy bleeding with large clots or tissue, significant cramping, tachycardia or orthostatic changes, falling hematocrit, or retained products with early infection
severity.critical: Hemorrhagic shock from heavy bleeding, or septic abortion with fever, uterine tenderness, foul discharge, hypotension and organ dysfunction

red_flags.finding: Heavy bleeding soaking more than one pad per hour, or passage of large clots
red_flags.meaning: Ongoing hemorrhage; assess hemodynamics and prepare for possible transfusion or urgent evacuation

red_flags.finding: Fever, chills, or foul-smelling vaginal discharge
red_flags.meaning: Septic abortion until proven otherwise; needs antibiotics and uterine evacuation

red_flags.finding: Severe unilateral pelvic pain, shoulder tip pain, or syncope
red_flags.meaning: Ectopic pregnancy with possible rupture; surgical emergency

red_flags.finding: Hypotension, tachycardia, pallor, or altered mental status
red_flags.meaning: Hypovolemic or septic shock; resuscitate immediately

red_flags.finding: Uterus larger than dates with very high hCG or passage of grapelike tissue
red_flags.meaning: Molar pregnancy; risk of persistent trophoblastic disease and need for follow-up

red_flags.finding: Open cervix with visible membranes or tissue in the second trimester
red_flags.meaning: Cervical insufficiency or inevitable loss; urgent obstetric evaluation

complications.name: Retained products of conception
clues: Persistent bleeding after passage of tissue
Ultrasound showing echogenic material within the uterus

complications.name: Disseminated intravascular coagulation
clues: Heavy bleeding with oozing from puncture sites
Prolonged PT, aPTT, and low fibrinogen

complications.name: Rh sensitization
clues: Rh-negative mother without anti-D immune globulin
Future pregnancy with hemolytic disease of the newborn

complications.name: Psychological grief and depression
clues: Persistent sadness, anxiety, or guilt after loss

complications.name: Asherman syndrome (intrauterine adhesions)
clues: History of repeated dilation and curettage
Amenorrhea or hypomenorrhea after the event

special_populations.differences: Women over 40 have a higher baseline risk of miscarriage and are more likely to have fibroids, chronic disease, or prior pregnancy loss; bleeding may be earlier or more subtle.

Poorly controlled diabetes increases miscarriage risk and can make bleeding and cramping harder to distinguish from other pregnancy complications; optimize glycemic control before and during pregnancy.
Obesity is associated with higher miscarriage risk and may make pelvic examination and ultrasound visualization more difficult.
Rh-negative women with bleeding should receive anti-D immune globulin; counseling and mental health support are important after loss.

key_questions.question: When was your last menstrual period, and how far along do you think you are?
key_questions.looking_for: Gestational age by dates; most miscarriages occur before 12 weeks

key_questions.question: When did the bleeding start, and how heavy is it now?
key_questions.looking_for: Spotting versus heavy bleeding; soaking more than one pad per hour suggests hemorrhage

key_questions.question: Have you passed any clots or tissue?
key_questions.looking_for: Passage of grayish or pinkish tissue suggests an incomplete or completed loss

key_questions.question: Do you have cramping or pain, and where is it?
key_questions.looking_for: Central crampy pelvic pain; severe unilateral pain suggests ectopic pregnancy

key_questions.question: Have you had any fever, chills, or foul-smelling discharge?
key_questions.looking_for: Suggests septic abortion, which needs antibiotics and uterine evacuation

key_questions.question: Have you had any shoulder tip pain, dizziness, or fainting?
key_questions.looking_for: Suggests ectopic pregnancy with rupture or significant blood loss

key_questions.question: Have you had an ultrasound or blood tests for this pregnancy yet?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior confirmation of an intrauterine pregnancy or prior hCG values

key_questions.question: Have you had a miscarriage or pregnancy loss before?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior loss raises risk and may suggest recurrent pregnancy loss

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, thyroid disease, or polycystic ovary syndrome?
key_questions.looking_for: Uncontrolled chronic disease increases miscarriage risk

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, drink alcohol, or use any drugs?
key_questions.looking_for: Modifiable risk factors for pregnancy loss

key_questions.question: Are you taking any medications, including misoprostol, methotrexate, warfarin, isotretinoin, or valproate?
key_questions.looking_for: Medications that can cause or complicate pregnancy loss

key_questions.question: Have you had any recent abdominal trauma or uterine procedures?
key_questions.looking_for: Trauma or instrumentation as a trigger for bleeding or loss

reasoning_points: Reproductive-age woman with a positive pregnancy test presenting with vaginal bleeding and cramping pelvic pain
Gestational age under 20 weeks, most commonly before 12 weeks
Passage of clots or tissue supports an incomplete or completed miscarriage
Pelvic exam showing blood in the vaginal vault, with an open or closed cervical os and possible tissue at the os
Quantitative serum hCG confirms pregnancy and serial values show a suboptimal rise or fall
Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus, an anembryonic sac, an embryo without cardiac activity, or retained products of conception
Ectopic pregnancy must be excluded, especially with unilateral pain, an empty uterus above the discriminatory zone, or hemodynamic instability
Fever, foul discharge, or uterine tenderness suggests septic abortion and requires urgent treatment
Rh-negative women with bleeding should receive anti-D immune globulin

easy: Reproductive-age woman with a positive pregnancy test and vaginal bleeding
Cramping pelvic pain with passage of clots or tissue
Transvaginal ultrasound showing an empty uterus or an embryo without cardiac activity
Closed or open cervix on pelvic exam consistent with the clinical stage
medium: Very early pregnancy with spotting and a nondiagnostic ultrasound
Closed cervix with a viable-appearing pregnancy on ultrasound (threatened miscarriage)
Need to distinguish miscarriage from ectopic pregnancy when the uterus is empty
Mild leukocytosis or blood on urinalysis causing diagnostic uncertainty
hard: Hemodynamically unstable patient with heavy bleeding and a falling hematocrit
Fever, foul discharge, and uterine tenderness suggesting septic abortion
Uterus larger than dates with very high hCG or passage of grapelike tissue suggesting molar pregnancy
Second-trimester painless cervical dilation suggesting cervical insufficiency
Obesity or fibroids making pelvic examination and ultrasound visualization difficult
